topics.name: Rate of Change of Quantities
topics.summary: This topic treats a derivative as an instantaneous rate of change: if a quantity \( y \) depends on \( x \), then \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) measures how fast \( y \) changes as \( x \) changes at a specific instant. Most questions involve a geometric or physical quantity (area, volume, distance travelled) expressed as a function of a single variable, which is then differentiated directly, or as a function of time when several quantities change together (\"related rates\"), which requires the chain rule. In related-rates problems, every quantity is first expressed in terms of a single variable using a geometric constraint, the whole equation is differentiated with respect to time, and only THEN are the known numerical values substituted \(-\) substituting too early is a common and serious error, since it silently turns variables into constants before differentiation. Typical contexts include expanding circles, growing spheres and cubes, draining or filling tanks, and moving points such as a ladder sliding down a wall.
key_formulas: \( \dfrac{dy}{dt}=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\cdot\dfrac{dx}{dt} \) (chain rule for related rates)
Circle: \( A=\pi r^2 \), \( \dfrac{dA}{dt}=2\pi r\dfrac{dr}{dt} \); \( C=2\pi r \), \( \dfrac{dC}{dt}=2\pi\dfrac{dr}{dt} \)
Sphere: \( V=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \), \( \dfrac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2\dfrac{dr}{dt} \); \( S=4\pi r^2 \), \( \dfrac{dS}{dt}=8\pi r\dfrac{dr}{dt} \)
Cube: \( V=x^3 \), \( \dfrac{dV}{dt}=3x^2\dfrac{dx}{dt} \)
Cylinder: \( V=\pi r^2h \) (differentiate with product rule if both \( r \) and \( h \) vary)
topics.worked_example:
A spherical balloon is being inflated so that its radius increases at \( \dfrac{dr}{dt}=2 \) cm/s. Find the rate at which its volume is increasing when \( r=5 \) cm.

\( V=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2\dfrac{dr}{dt} \). At \( r=5 \): \( \dfrac{dV}{dt}=4\pi(25)(2)=200\pi \) cm\(^3\)/s.
common_mistakes: Substituting the known numerical values BEFORE differentiating, which turns a variable into a constant and gives a derivative of zero for it
Forgetting to apply the chain rule when a quantity depends on time only through another variable (writing \( dV/dt=4\pi r^2 \) instead of \( 4\pi r^2\,dr/dt \))
Confusing which rate is being asked for (e.g. finding \( dr/dt \) when the question asks for \( dA/dt \), or vice versa)
Dropping the power-rule coefficient when differentiating (e.g. using \( dV/dx=x^2 \) instead of \( 3x^2 \) for \( V=x^3 \))

topics.name: Increasing and Decreasing Functions
topics.summary: A function \( f \) is increasing on an interval where \( f'(x)>0 \) throughout, and decreasing where \( f'(x)<0 \) throughout. The standard method is to find the critical points (where \( f'(x)=0 \) or is undefined), use them to split the domain into intervals, and test the SIGN of \( f' \) at one sample point inside each interval. A subtle but important nuance is that a single isolated zero of \( f' \) does not necessarily break monotonicity: if \( f'(x)\ge0 \) everywhere and equals zero only at one isolated point (typically from a repeated factor like \( x^2 \)), the function can still be strictly increasing overall, since the sign never actually flips. This topic underlies the FIRST DERIVATIVE TEST used throughout Maxima and Minima: a critical point where \( f' \) changes sign from positive to negative is a local maximum, and from negative to positive is a local minimum.
key_formulas: \( f \) increasing on an interval \( \iff f'(x)>0 \) throughout it
\( f \) decreasing on an interval \( \iff f'(x)<0 \) throughout it
First derivative test: \( f' \) changes \( + \to - \) at \( c \) \( \Rightarrow \) local maximum at \( c \); \( f' \) changes \( - \to + \) at \( c \) \( \Rightarrow \) local minimum at \( c \)
An isolated zero of \( f' \) (no sign change around it) is NOT an extremum
topics.worked_example:
Find the intervals of increase and decrease of \( f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+5 \).

\( f'(x)=3x^2-6x-9=3(x-3)(x+1) \). Sign chart: positive on \( (-\infty,-1) \), negative on \( (-1,3) \), positive on \( (3,\infty) \). So \( f \) is increasing on \( (-\infty,-1)\cup(3,\infty) \) and decreasing on \( (-1,3) \).
common_mistakes: Assuming every zero of \( f'(x) \) is automatically a local extremum, without checking that the sign of \( f' \) actually changes there
Building the sign chart backwards (mixing up which interval is positive and which is negative)
Testing only the critical points' \( x \)-values without picking an actual sample point inside each interval
Treating 'increasing at a point' and 'increasing on an interval' as interchangeable when the derivative is zero at an isolated point

topics.name: Tangents and Normals to a Curve
topics.summary: The tangent line to a curve \( y=f(x) \) at a point \( (x_0,y_0) \) has slope \( m=f'(x_0) \), and its equation is \( y-y_0=m(x-x_0) \). The NORMAL is the line perpendicular to the tangent at the same point, so its slope is \( -\dfrac{1}{m} \) (for \( m\neq0 \)) \(-\) never \( m \) itself, and never the plain reciprocal without the sign flip. A special case that is easy to miss: if the tangent is horizontal (\( m=0 \)), the normal is not given by any reciprocal formula at all \(-\) it becomes the VERTICAL line through that point. Typical problems ask for tangents/normals at a given point, at points where the tangent is parallel or perpendicular to a given line, or where the tangent passes through an external point not on the curve.
key_formulas: If \( f'(x_0)=0 \): tangent is \( y=y_0 \) (horizontal); normal is \( x=x_0 \) (vertical)
Two lines are parallel when their slopes are equal, and perpendicular when the product of their slopes is \( -1 \)
topics.worked_example:
Find the equations of the tangent and normal to \( y=x^2 \) at \( x=2 \).

\( y'=2x \), so \( y'(2)=4 \) and \( y(2)=4 \). Tangent: \( y-4=4(x-2)\Rightarrow y=4x-4 \). Normal: slope \( =-\dfrac{1}{4} \), so \( y-4=-\dfrac{1}{4}(x-2)\Rightarrow y=-\dfrac{1}{4}x+\dfrac{9}{2} \).
common_mistakes: Using the tangent's slope \( m \) directly as the normal's slope, instead of \( -1/m \)
Using the plain reciprocal \( 1/m \) for the normal's slope without flipping the sign
Forgetting that when \( m=0 \), the normal is a vertical line, not an undefined or non-existent one
Writing the point-slope equation with a sign error, e.g. \( y+y_0=m(x-x_0) \) instead of \( y-y_0=m(x-x_0) \)

topics.name: Approximations Using Differentials
topics.summary: For a small change \( dx=\Delta x \) in \( x \), the actual change in \( y=f(x) \) can be approximated using the differential \( dy=f'(x)\,dx \), so that \( f(x+\Delta x)\approx f(x)+f'(x)\,\Delta x \). This is the equation of the tangent line at \( x \), evaluated at the nearby point \( x+\Delta x \) \(-\) geometrically, the tangent line is used as a stand-in for the curve over a very short distance. This is the one place in the chapter where small decimal values (like \( 0.1 \) or \( 0.01 \)) are expected and correct, since the whole method relies on \( \Delta x \) being small. A closely related application is error and percentage-error estimation: if a measured quantity has a small error \( dx \), the resulting error in a dependent quantity is estimated the same way, and the percentage error is \( \dfrac{dy}{y}\times100\% \).
key_formulas: \( dy=f'(x)\,dx \) and \( f(x+dx)\approx f(x)+dy \)
Percentage error in \( y \): \( \dfrac{dy}{y}\times100\% \)
For \( y=x^n \): a percentage error \( p\% \) in \( x \) gives approximately \( np\% \) error in \( y \)
At a critical point (\( f'(x_0)=0 \)), the differential \( dy=0 \), so the first-order approximation predicts NO change there
topics.worked_example:
Use a differential to approximate \( \sqrt{25.3} \).

Let \( f(x)=\sqrt{x} \), \( x=25 \), \( dx=0.3 \). \( f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \), so \( f'(25)=\dfrac{1}{10} \). \( \sqrt{25.3}\approx5+\dfrac{1}{10}(0.3)=5.03 \).
common_mistakes: Adding \( \Delta x \) directly to \( f(x) \) without scaling it by \( f'(x) \) first
Using the wrong sign of \( \Delta x \) (subtracting instead of adding, or vice versa) when the new point is on the other side of the base point
Forgetting that the differential approximation gives ZERO change when the base point is a critical point of the function
Confusing an absolute error \( dy \) with a percentage error \( dy/y\times100\% \)

topics.name: Maxima and Minima: First and Second Derivative Tests, and Absolute Extrema on a Closed Interval
topics.summary: A function's LOCAL extrema occur at critical points, where \( f'(x)=0 \) (or is undefined). The SECOND DERIVATIVE TEST classifies such a point \( c \): if \( f''(c)>0 \), \( c \) is a local MINIMUM; if \( f''(c)<0 \), \( c \) is a local MAXIMUM \(-\) the reverse of what is often guessed. When \( f''(c)=0 \) or is inconclusive, the FIRST DERIVATIVE TEST (sign change of \( f' \) around \( c \)) is used instead. For the ABSOLUTE (global) maximum or minimum of a continuous function on a CLOSED interval \( [a,b] \), it is not enough to find local extrema: EVERY critical point in \( [a,b] \) and BOTH endpoints \( a \) and \( b \) must be evaluated and compared \(-\) stopping at \( f'(x)=0 \) alone is incomplete, and the true extremum can sometimes lie only at an endpoint, or even tie between an endpoint and an interior point. This topic also covers classic optimization word problems (maximum area, minimum surface area, and similar) solved by expressing the target quantity as a function of one variable and applying these same tests.
key_formulas: Critical points: solve \( f'(x)=0 \)
Second derivative test: \( f''(c)>0\Rightarrow \) local minimum; \( f''(c)<0\Rightarrow \) local maximum
First derivative test: sign of \( f' \) changes \( + \to - \Rightarrow \) local maximum; \( - \to + \Rightarrow \) local minimum
Absolute extrema on \( [a,b] \): compare \( f(a) \), \( f(b) \), and \( f(c) \) for every critical point \( c\in[a,b] \)
topics.worked_example:
Find the absolute maximum and minimum of \( f(x)=x^3-3x \) on \( [-2,3] \).

\( f'(x)=3x^2-3=0\Rightarrow x=\pm1 \), both in \( [-2,3] \). \( f(-2)=-2,\ f(-1)=2,\ f(1)=-2,\ f(3)=18,\ f(2)... \) checking all: \( f(-2)=-2,\ f(-1)=2,\ f(1)=-2,\ f(3)=18 \). Absolute maximum \( =18 \) at \( x=3 \); absolute minimum \( =-2 \) (tied at \( x=-2 \) and \( x=1 \)).
common_mistakes: Misreading the second derivative test: treating \( f''(c)>0 \) as a maximum or \( f''(c)<0 \) as a minimum
For absolute extrema on a closed interval, checking only the critical points and forgetting to also evaluate both endpoints
For absolute extrema, checking only the endpoints and forgetting an interior critical point
Assuming every point where \( f'(x)=0 \) must be an extremum, without confirming with either derivative test
